title: Projecting precipitation extremes over Cyprus using CMIP6 climate scenarios
abstract: Changing climatic conditions have significant consequences for precipitation extremes, especially in water-limited regions, such as Cyprus in the Eastern Mediterranean. This study evaluates historical and future extreme precipitation using twenty-three models from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6). The simulations are validated against the Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Stations dataset (CHIRPS) and combined with bias-corrected projections produced through Quantile Delta Mapping (QDM) under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. According to performance evaluations of models, MRI-ESM2-0 and EC-Earth3-Veg-LR stand out as the top-performing models for capturing extreme precipitation behavior over the island. Furthermore, the results suggest a long-term decrease in total precipitation and in the number of moderate and heavy precipitation days toward the end of the century under both scenarios. At the same time, 1-day precipitation maximum generally intensify over most of the island under both scenarios, whereas 5-day precipitation maximum increase under SSP2-4.5 but decline under SSP5-8.5 toward the end of the century. High-percentile indices also strengthen, which indicates a future climate where fewer but more powerful events make up a larger share of annual precipitation. The duration-based indices also lead to an increase in consecutive dry days and shorter wet periods toward the end of the century under high emission scenario, which together signal a shift toward more prolonged dryness and more severe drought events. These combined changes imply that Cyprus will face greater stress on its water resources and experience greater flood risks associated with more intense events. The results also highlight the importance of region-specific strategies that can improve the resilience of water resources under changing climatic conditions.
problem: Research on precipitation extremes in Cyprus is limited, with no prior studies utilizing the improved CMIP6 global climate models to project future changes for this highly vulnerable Mediterranean island, creating a significant knowledge gap.
method: The paper projects future precipitation extremes by bias-correcting CMIP6 climate models using Quantile Delta Mapping against CHIRPS data, then creating a weighted multi-model ensemble based on performance evaluation to analyze trends under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios over Cyprus.
task: The task is to evaluate and project future precipitation extremes over Cyprus using twenty-three CMIP6 climate models under the SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios.
innovation: This study provides the first detailed assessment of historical and future precipitation extremes over Cyprus using an ensemble of twenty-three bias-corrected CMIP6 global climate models under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios.

CMIP6 Global Climate Models are employed to analyze both historical and future climate conditions. Daily precipitation outputs from 23 CMIP6 GCMs are used for the historical period (1981–2010) and for three future time frames: near-term (2025–2049), mid-term (2050–2074), and far-term (2075–2099), defined as hydrological years, under two Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5).

However, the projected decline in Mediterranean cyclone frequency (Flaounas et al. 2022) may reduce multi-day precipitation accumulations, leading to widespread Rx5day decline under the high-emission scenario toward the end of the century.

In the Troodos Mountains, where topography produces a steep precipitation gradient from approximately 300 mm on the lowland plains to up to 1000 mm in the mountains (Hadjinicolaou et al. 2011; Ghanem and Zaifoglu 2024), the projected weakening of Cyprus Lows (Hochman et al. 2018; Zittis et al. 2022) may reduce moisture transport to high elevations sufficiently that even 1-day precipitation maximum decline toward the end of the century alongside 5-day precipitation.

The intensity of extreme precipitation increases over most of the Cyprus, especially under SSP5-8.5, which shows that short lasting intense events become more severe. Higher Rx1day values lead to higher peak flows, faster runoff, and a greater risk of flash floods, especially in steep or urban areas.
